exhibits.title: The Industrial Revolution

when.display: Britain c. 1760–1840; spreading worldwide through the 19th century

exhibits.change: Machines powered by coal began to do the work of muscle — and output per person started to grow year after year.
exhibits.context: Textile machinery, coke-smelted iron, steam engines and the factory system combined in Britain, drawing on global trade (including cotton grown by enslaved people) and cheap coal. For the first time in history, sustained economic growth outpaced population growth — but early industrial cities were crowded, polluted and dangerous, and child labour was common.
exhibits.significance: The pivot between an agrarian world and the modern one: mass production, fossil energy, urbanisation, and the start of human-driven climate change.

uncertainty.note: Why it began in Britain, and how gradual it was, are long-running debates among economic historians.

sources.note: Our World in Data page is general background only.

exhibits.title: Steam Power

when.display: 1769 (separate condenser patent); rotative engines from the 1780s

exhibits.change: Heat became reliable, portable, rotary power for any machine.
exhibits.context: James Watt's separate condenser cut fuel use dramatically; with Matthew Boulton he built engines that turned wheels, driving mills, factories and later locomotives and ships. John Wilkinson's precise cylinder boring made them possible.
exhibits.significance: The first general-purpose power source not tied to rivers, wind or muscle.

exhibits.title: The Factory
exhibits.change: Workers and machines brought under one roof, running to the clock.
exhibits.context: Richard Arkwright's water-powered spinning mill at Cromford ran in shifts with hundreds of workers, many of them children. The model spread to steam-powered mills in the cities.
exhibits.significance: A new organisation of work that shaped the modern economy.

sources.note: UNESCO World Heritage: Derwent Valley Mills.

exhibits.title: Interchangeable Parts

when.display: demonstrated in France c. 1778–1790; the 'American system' by the 1820s

exhibits.change: Parts made so precisely that any one would fit any machine.
exhibits.context: French gunsmith Honoré Blanc demonstrated interchangeable musket locks; US armories developed machine tools and gauges to make parts interchangeable in practice by the 1820s.
exhibits.significance: The prerequisite for mass production, repair by replacement, and modern supply chains.

exhibits.title: The First Human Flight
exhibits.change: People rose into the sky in a hot-air balloon.
exhibits.context: The Montgolfier brothers' balloon carried Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes over Paris in November 1783; a hydrogen balloon flew days later.
exhibits.significance: The first human flight — lighter than air, at the mercy of the wind.

exhibits.title: Modern Chemistry
exhibits.change: Elements, compounds and conservation of mass replaced the old theory of phlogiston.
exhibits.context: Antoine Lavoisier, working with Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, used careful weighing to show combustion is combination with oxygen, and listed chemical elements in his Traité élémentaire de chimie.
exhibits.significance: Chemistry became a quantitative science — the basis of industry, medicine and materials.

exhibits.title: Vaccination
exhibits.change: Cowpox protected against smallpox — safely.
exhibits.context: Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox and showed he was then immune to smallpox. Vaccination spread worldwide within a decade, including a Spanish expedition that carried it to the Americas and Asia (1803–1806).
exhibits.significance: The first vaccine — and the path to eradicating smallpox 184 years later.

exhibits.title: The Battery
exhibits.change: A pile of metal discs and brine produced a steady electric current.
exhibits.context: Alessandro Volta's pile, answering Galvani's experiments with frogs, gave scientists continuous current for the first time. Within weeks it was used to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
exhibits.significance: Electricity could now be studied and used — the start of electrochemistry and electromagnetism.

exhibits.title: The Jacquard Loom
exhibits.change: Chains of punched cards told a loom which threads to lift.
exhibits.context: Joseph-Marie Jacquard's attachment, building on earlier French devices, let complex patterns be woven automatically from stored instructions.
exhibits.significance: A stored program controlling a machine — Babbage borrowed the idea for his Analytical Engine.

exhibits.title: The Locomotive
exhibits.change: A steam engine on wheels pulled its own load along rails.
exhibits.context: Richard Trevithick's high-pressure engine hauled iron on a tramway in 1804. George and Robert Stephenson's Rocket (1829) established the design of steam locomotives.
exhibits.significance: Land transport faster than a horse, for the first time.

exhibits.title: Surgical Anaesthesia
exhibits.change: Surgery without consciousness of pain.
exhibits.context: Hanaoka Seishū performed a mastectomy under a herbal general anaesthetic in 1804, but his method stayed in Japan. The public demonstration of ether in Boston in 1846 spread anaesthesia worldwide within months.
exhibits.significance: Made long, careful operations possible.

exhibits.title: Atomic Theory
exhibits.change: Each element made of identical atoms with a characteristic weight.
exhibits.context: John Dalton explained fixed proportions in chemical compounds with atoms of different weights. Ancient atomism in Greece and India had been philosophy; this was quantitative science.
exhibits.significance: The foundation of chemistry's structure — and a century later, of atomic physics.

exhibits.title: Thermodynamics
exhibits.change: The laws of heat and work: energy is conserved, and disorder grows.
exhibits.context: Sadi Carnot analysed the limits of heat engines; Mayer, Joule and Helmholtz established conservation of energy; Clausius and Kelvin formulated the second law and entropy.
exhibits.significance: Explains engines, refrigerators, stars and the direction of time.

exhibits.title: Railways
exhibits.change: Scheduled steam trains shrank countries into days.
exhibits.context: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was the first inter-city line with scheduled passenger trains, all steam-hauled. Within fifty years railways crossed continents; standardised time zones were created to run them.
exhibits.significance: Mass travel, national markets and standard time.

exhibits.title: Photography
exhibits.change: Light fixed an image on a chemical surface.
exhibits.context: Nicéphore Niépce's view from a window is the oldest surviving camera photograph. Daguerre's process (1839) produced sharp unique images; Talbot's paper negatives allowed copies.
exhibits.significance: A new kind of evidence — and the ancestor of cinema, X-ray imaging and digital cameras.

exhibits.title: Electromagnetic Induction
exhibits.change: A moving magnet made current flow in a wire.
exhibits.context: Michael Faraday discovered induction and built the first dynamo and electric motor demonstrations; Joseph Henry made similar discoveries in America.
exhibits.significance: Every generator and electric motor rests on it.

exhibits.title: The Electric Telegraph
exhibits.change: Messages travelled at the speed of electricity.
exhibits.context: Electric telegraphs were developed in parallel in several countries. Morse code and a single-wire system became the international standard; lines followed the railways.
exhibits.significance: Information separated from transport for the first time — the beginning of telecommunications.

exhibits.title: The Analytical Engine
exhibits.change: The design of a general-purpose, programmable computer — in brass and steam.
exhibits.context: Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine had a 'store', a 'mill' and punched-card programs. Ada Lovelace's notes include an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers and the insight that such machines could manipulate symbols, not only numbers. It was never built.
exhibits.significance: The concept of the computer, a century early.

sources.note: Computer History Museum overview is general background.

exhibits.title: Drilling for Oil
exhibits.change: Wells drilled for petroleum opened a new, dense source of energy.
exhibits.context: An exploratory oil well was drilled near Baku in 1846; Edwin Drake's 1859 well in Pennsylvania launched the American oil industry. Kerosene for lamps came first; petrol and diesel later.
exhibits.significance: Fuel for the automobile age, plastics and petrochemicals — and a major source of carbon emissions.

exhibits.title: Cheap Steel

regions.note: William Kelly developed a similar process.

exhibits.change: Air blown through molten iron made steel in minutes, not days.
exhibits.context: Henry Bessemer's converter, followed by the Siemens–Martin open-hearth process, made steel cheap enough for rails, ships, bridges and skyscrapers.
exhibits.significance: The structural material of the modern world.

exhibits.title: Germ Theory

regions.note: Semmelweis in Vienna; Koch in Berlin.

exhibits.change: Many diseases are caused by specific microorganisms.
exhibits.context: Semmelweis showed handwashing prevented childbed fever; Snow traced cholera to a water pump; Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation; Koch identified the bacteria of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera.
exhibits.significance: Clean water, sanitation, sterile surgery and vaccines followed — life expectancy began to rise dramatically.

exhibits.title: Evolution by Natural Selection

regions.note: Wallace reached the idea independently in the Malay Archipelago.

exhibits.change: All living things share ancestry and change through natural selection.
exhibits.context: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently arrived at natural selection; their papers were presented together in 1858. Evidence from fossils, anatomy and, later, genetics has confirmed common descent.
exhibits.significance: The unifying theory of biology — and the framework in which this Museum's first galleries make sense.

exhibits.title: The Transatlantic Cable
exhibits.change: Messages between Europe and America in minutes instead of weeks.
exhibits.context: The 1866 cable, laid by the steamship Great Eastern, worked reliably. Kelvin's physics of signal transmission was essential.
exhibits.significance: The start of near-instant global communication.

exhibits.title: Maxwell's Equations
exhibits.change: Electricity, magnetism and light turned out to be one thing.
exhibits.context: James Clerk Maxwell unified electric and magnetic fields and predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light. Heinrich Hertz generated them in 1887.
exhibits.significance: Radio, radar, television, mobile phones and Wi-Fi follow from these equations.

exhibits.title: The Laws of Heredity
exhibits.change: Traits pass on as discrete units in predictable ratios.
exhibits.context: Gregor Mendel's pea experiments were overlooked until 1900, when three botanists rediscovered them. Combined with Darwin's theory they formed modern genetics.
exhibits.significance: The foundation of genetics and modern plant and animal breeding.

exhibits.title: Antiseptic Surgery
exhibits.change: Carbolic acid on wounds and instruments cut deaths after surgery.
exhibits.context: Joseph Lister applied Pasteur's germ theory to surgery; antisepsis later gave way to aseptic technique (sterile everything).
exhibits.significance: Together with anaesthesia, it made modern surgery possible.

exhibits.title: The Periodic Table
exhibits.change: The elements fell into a pattern — with gaps for ones not yet found.
exhibits.context: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic weight and properties and predicted gallium, scandium and germanium, all later discovered. Lothar Meyer produced a similar table independently.
exhibits.significance: Chemistry's map; later explained by atomic structure.

exhibits.title: The Suez Canal
exhibits.change: A sea-level canal joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
exhibits.context: Dug largely by forced Egyptian labour in its early years, the canal cut the sea route from Europe to Asia by thousands of kilometres.
exhibits.significance: A chokepoint of global trade ever since.
